After my parinirvāṇa, the veneration of the śarīra shall remain as it was before."

If a virtuous person writes this sutra, studies, maintains, recites, takes refuge in it, pays homage, and serves and makes offerings to it in full accordance with what was previously described, they will thereby have made offerings to the Omniscient One and shall obtain incomparable merit from this sutra.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for the people of Jambudvīpa who do not make offerings, is it because they do not know that this merit is supreme and peerless?
The Buddha said:
"How many people are there who believe in the Buddha, believe in the Sūtras, and believe in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus?
Śāriputra replied, "Those who believe are few indeed; even fewer are those who seek the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, up to those who seek Buddhahood."
The Buddha said:
"Innumerable people practice seeking the path of the Buddha, yet those who have reached the stage of non-retrogression are but one or two.
Those who study this Dharma will surely attain Buddhahood; you should pay them homage, serve them, and revere them."
Why is this? Because those who understand the Buddha-dharma are rare in the world.
All Tathāgatas of the past who sought the path of Buddhahood achieved it through this, and I was also among them at that time.

After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, one constructs a stupa of the seven precious jewels from his relics, and throughout one's entire life, takes refuge in him, pays homage, serves, and makes offerings—complete with celestial jewels, flowers, and incense, all as described before—filling the four continents; or if all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm were to attain the human path and each construct a stupa of the seven precious jewels, providing them with music and entertainment.

Furthermore, suppose one were to pass beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges River, and every person therein were to erect stupas made of the seven treasures to make offerings for kalpa after kalpa—provided with all the musical performances, flowers, incense, silken canopies, and so forth found within the desire realm as previously described—would not their merit be even greater?
He replied,
"Very many, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"It would be better to write out and uphold this sutra scroll, for the merit of self-reliance and meditative protection is immeasurably greater. Why is this?
Because from within it emerges the all-knowing wisdom of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said:
"Even if people were to erect stupas made of the seven treasures for as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in a hundred times the Ganges River, this would not even enter into calculation.
Even if it were increased by thousands of millions of billions of countless times, it would still not enter into the calculation of the pure concentration of the Perfection of Wisdom."
At that time, forty thousand devaputras came to the great assembly together with Śakra. Those devaputras addressed Śakra, saying:
"Venerable One!
You should take up and recite this sutra."
The Buddha said:
"You should train in it, uphold it, and recite it,
O Śākya!"
If the spirit Zhiliang raises an army with the intent to wage war against the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by reciting this sutra, the host of spirits Zhiliang will immediately depart.
Śakra said:
“Great Honored One’s mantra!
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said: "Indeed!"
O Celestial Beings!
All Buddhas of the ten directions—past, future, and present—all give rise to this mantra, thereby attaining Buddhahood for themselves and manifesting the ten merits of sincerity.

From within this, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are born. When the Buddha has not yet appeared in the world, these Bodhisattvas all emerge to preach, illuminating the four abandonments, the four [truths], the four matters for uprooting suffering, and the five supernormal powers of emptiness.
For example, when the moon is at its fullness, it emerges from the sky and illuminates the stars.
In this same way, when a bodhisattva seeks the fullness of merit, it all emerges from the great radiance of skillful means and virtue.
"You should understand it thus: by studying, upholding, and reciting this sutra, one will be fully endowed with supreme virtue.
The Buddha said, "Such a person shall never suffer an untimely death from evil poisons, water, fire, weapons, or the laws of kings."
Why is this? Because they are protected by this Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, if other matters arise, whether they go before a king, a crown prince, or a high minister, whenever they meet them, they will immediately speak with joy and laughter.

"Why is this so? It is because his universal compassion, impartial salvation, and benevolent grace toward all living beings bring forth immeasurable merit and function; therefore, all who see him rise to their feet.
At that time, there was a heterodox practitioner who, seeing from afar the Buddha’s great assembly, wished to disrupt and disturb those seated, and quickly approached the place where the Buddha was.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"How can I spend the remainder of my life receiving and reciting this Dharma from the Buddha?
He then received and recited it directly from the Buddha.
That heterodox practitioner circumambulated the God among Gods from afar once and departed by a side path.
Śāriputra thought:
"How is it that this heterodox practitioner has departed by a side path?"
As he thought this, the Buddha immediately knew:
"Son of Autumn Dew!
Śāriputra is contemplating the Perfection of Wisdom."
Because heterodox practitioners have come with no benevolent intent, they harbor evil and depraved thoughts:

"The Buddha is seated together with his fourfold assembly; the gods of the desire realm, the Brahmā heavens, and all the sons of heaven are likewise present among them. There is no one else in this gathering except for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have received their predictions, who shall become leaders among men and attain Buddhahood themselves."
"I shall go and disturb him.
Then this wicked Māra mounted a single-axle chariot drawn by four horses and gradually approached the place where the Buddha was.
Śakra thought to himself:

"Ridden by Māra the Wicked, this is not King Bimbisāra’s, nor King Prasenajit’s, nor that of the Śākya clan, nor the four-horse chariot of Vaiśālī; it is none of these, but is indeed the work of Māra the Wicked."
"The wicked ones constantly seek out the Buddha's shortcomings day and night, creating chaos for the people of this world.
If one can always maintain the mind and bring the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Ultimate Perfection of Wisdom) to completion, the wicked will then turn back on their path.
Then, the Devaputra Kāyika-ga-yi stood in mid-air holding celestial flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; scattering them from all four sides, he praised him with reverence, saying:
“The ultimate source of the Way is what is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
May the people of Jambudvīpa be able to hear and behold it.
He then took various flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, saying:
"Those who seek [this teaching] and those who guard it will never be harmed by wicked multitudes.
Such people possess vast and great merit; how much more so for those who study, uphold, recite, and abide by this Dharma."
That person has already encountered a Buddha in previous lives and made offerings with a pure mind.
Desiring all-knowledge and seeking the jewel of omniscience, they should seek it from the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
The Buddha said, "Indeed!
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"One does not mention the names of giving, the observance of precepts, patience, diligence, or the abandonment of meditative concentration, but mentions only the name of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
Why is this so, O God among Gods?
The Buddha said:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the most honored among all perfections.
What do you think, Ānanda?"
Should one who does not practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom take these as the conditions for the six perfections and all-knowledge?
Ānanda said:
"Indeed it is so, O God among Gods!

If one does not practice the six modes of conduct and does not cultivate the six perfections, it is truly not the Great Perfection of Wisdom (Mahāprajñāpāramitā); this is clearly known by the All-Knowing One."
The Buddha said:
"Indeed! The Great Illumination is most supreme."
It is like the earth: when seeds are sown within it, they sprout simultaneously, and sentient beings obtain their lives.
In this same way, Ānanda!
The Perfection of Wisdom is like the earth, and the five perfections are like the seeds; from within it, they are produced and brought to completion.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The merit of the noble person who studies, maintains, and recites the Prajñāpāramitā, as spoken by the Tathāgata, is not yet exhausted.
The Buddha said to Śakra:

"I do not say that these merits are incomplete; rather, I am speaking only of the merits of those who copy and uphold this sutra, and who honor it with offerings, prostrations, flowers, incense, precious jewels, various silken canopies, and banners."
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I shall personally guard and watch over this person.
The Buddha said to Śakra:

"When one recites the Prajñāpāramitā, several thousands of devas will come to the teacher of this sutra; though they listen to the sutra without yet understanding its meaning and wish to ask about their doubts, through their compassion for the sutra, they will immediately attain clear realization on their own."
This person performs meritorious deeds and perceives them all for themselves.
When preaching the sutras among the fourfold assembly of disciples, their mind knows no hesitation, and they never fear those who might test them through physical means.
"Why is this? Because those protected by the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) are freed from malevolent trials.
The Buddha said:
“I do not perceive anyone who should be enlightened by the Perfection of Wisdom, nor do I perceive the Perfection of Wisdom, nor that which is weary of the Perfection of Wisdom.
There is no one who is slighted; the mind is without terror and has nothing to fear.”
Their parents value them; the śramaṇas take pity on them; and their kinsmen and virtuous friends love them.
Should any evil come upon them, they uphold the dharma of loyalty and rectitude to resolve it.
One should understand that all the merits performed by such virtuous persons are fully visible within their own minds.

In the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, devas, humans, ghosts, nāgas, *piśācas*, *gandharvas*, *kumbhāṇḍas*, and beings with human-like forms all come to the place of the scripture-master to inquire after his well-being, listen to and receive the teachings, pay homage with respect, circumambulate him, and then each depart.
This was due to the power of his conduct and virtue.

The Great Kings of the Four Heavenly Kingdoms, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmā Heaven, Brahmakāyika Heaven, Brahmapurohita Heaven, Mahābrahmā Heaven; the Ābhāsvara Heaven, Parīttābha Heaven, Apramāṇābha Heaven, Ābhāsvara Heaven; the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, Parīttaśubha Heaven, Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; the Vṛhatphala Heaven, Avṛha Heaven, Atapa Heaven, Sudṛśa Heaven, Sudarśana Heaven, and the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—all these sons of the gods went to inquire after his well-being, listened to his teachings, paid their respects, circumambulated him, and then departed.

If even the gods who are free from fetters and craving all descend and dwell among the other devas, how much more so must this be for the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the formless realm within this trichiliocosm?
The place where he dwells is always intact and firm, and no one can disturb it.
Except for that which was not requested in past lives, nothing else can move it.
He fully receives all its merits.
"At that time, when the devas come, you shall know it.
Śakra asked: "How will one know?"
"O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"When these good men and women feel joy, they know it; when they have arrived, one should avoid them, and when they depart, one smells the fragrance of the spirits."
If dragons, ghosts, spirits, or snake-bodied deities arrive and smell the fragrance of the ghost-spirits, they will think, "He already knows us," and they shall depart.
One should purify the body; because of this purity, the ghosts and spirits will all be greatly delighted.
When the minor devas saw the Great Deva approaching, they immediately withdrew.
The Great Deva’s majestic spiritual power was sublime and his radiance was doubly brilliant; he proceeded slowly and with composure.
When the Great Deva entered the place where the sutra was being recited, those virtuous men and women leaped for joy.

Wherever one dwells, one shall always abide in purity; such a person’s body will never be afflicted by illness, and their dwelling place will always be peaceful and secure. They shall never experience bad dreams; in their dreams, they see only Buddhas, see stupas, and hear the Prajñāpāramitā. They see only the disciples, see those who have attained ultimate transcendence, see the Buddha seated, see the spontaneous wheel of the Dharma, see the time when [the practitioner] is about to attain Buddhahood, see various Buddhas attaining Buddhahood, see the spontaneous new wheel of the Dharma, see various bodhisattvas, see the six perfections being explained in various ways with the declaration that they shall become Buddhas, see other buddha-fields, and see the Buddhas and their sublime scriptures as peerless. By means of what kind of giving?

to take all the merits of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as those disciples who have not yet attained the Way, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits who have first resolved their minds upon learning the Sūtra, and to rejoice in them all collectively throughout successive generations—this is most supreme.

The bodhisattva clarifies it in this way.

Regarding those whom the Buddhas have brought to parinirvāṇa, one should take the merit of what has been bestowed and cause oneself to obtain it all equally. Until one has attained the *prajñāpāramitā*, one cannot enter into these dharmas. Within the various virtues one maintains, do not allow the consciousness of the body to arise in such a way as to listen [to them].

These virtuous persons, possessing conceptualization, become attached and instead desire to dwell in suffering; the Tathāgata, who has attained the unattached, true, and perfect enlightenment, does not delight in the holding and giving of gifts, for he perceives the holding and giving of gifts as being like empty space.

The Tathāgata bestows [this gift] with full awareness. Why is this?

A person of such virtue should cultivate this realization:
"How did the Buddhas of the past, future, and present give gifts?
By what causes did they achieve and emerge in the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
"Following the Tathāgata’s instruction, I shall uphold this and bestow it, knowing the merit performed and the physical marks at the time of birth.

It shall never depart from the Dharma of the Tathāgata, nor shall it be mixed with poison.

One should practice giving in this manner: as is the case with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; as is the manifestation of the body through wisdom, which abides neither in the realm of desire, nor in the realm of form, nor in the realm of emptiness, and from which there is no one who comes from the past, goes to the future, or arrives from the present.
For example, just as there is nothing that exists, so too are all phenomena that are given likewise non-existent; this constitutes the absence of poison within the perfection of giving.
If one performs a different kind of giving, it becomes a perverse practice of giving.
"Only that which is bestowed by a bodhisattva is this Dharma, which is like that of a Buddha.

To act as one does for a Buddha;
furthermore, to cause all the people of the three thousand great world-systems to contemplate the four immeasurable minds is not equal to the aforementioned supreme, unsurpassed giving.

"The merit of rejoicing on behalf of others surpasses that [of the original deed]. Shan-ye said:
“Merits such as those would fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet they could not contain them.

“Excellent, excellent!”

For what reason is there no regression and no confusion?

O God among Gods!
If one harbors such thoughts and conceptions, they do not seek the Great Illumination.

The person is fundamentally non-existent, and the great illumination is likewise non-existent; the person does not perish, and the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom is thus. The power from which the person is born is such that the manifested power of the Tathāgata is also like this.

This cessation is for the sake of ceasing all-knowing, and for the sake of ceasing the guidance of the clear-eyed ones throughout the past and the future.

Śāriputra said to the Buddha, “The gravity of that offense is equal to the five heinous crimes; I have merely used a subtle analogy.

Those who obstruct others in their study ruin themselves and ruin others; they drink poison themselves and make others drink it as well. Such people, having perished themselves and lacking understanding of the *prajñāpāramitā*, further mislead others.

"These are the four matters.

The World-Honored One said, "Indeed!

“As the Buddha has taught, one should depart from all attachments.

You, as a bodhisattva mahāsattva, rely on emptiness and do not cling.

The Buddha said:
"These good men and women shall obtain merit that is vast and difficult to calculate. Why is this so?

Because the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) has no dharma to which it is near, no sūtra to be grasped; it is without existence or attainment, without flaw or blemish, without seeking and without conceptualization. The sons of the gods were filled with great joy in their hearts and, with one voice, exclaimed:

All that is produced from the various sūtras is like space: it neither revolves nor departs. To speak in this manner is to speak the sūtras.
There is no one who speaks the sūtras, no one who hears them, and no one who realizes them.
"One who preaches this sutra attains parinirvāṇa; one who preaches this sutra does so because there is no person.

O God among Gods!

they are without attachment and without body, without going and without coming, without existence and without sustenance, without exhaustion and without root, without origin and without cessation. They are...

like an illusion, it is without sight; like a dream, it is without self; pure and undefiled, invisible and placeless;
fixed and unshakable, equanimous in thought, the unmoving dharma that does not shift.

It is neither corrupt nor decaying, there is nothing it does not penetrate, and it is that which is not attained by the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
It is capable of reaching [all], undisturbed, unerring, and immeasurable; it contains no minor dharmas, is formless, has no origination, and is without suffering.

All dharmas have no point of emergence; their power is invincible, incalculable, transcending all calculation, and free from fear, with a mind that never slackens.
The Tathāgata’s dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, without teacher, unconditioned, and tranquil—this is the Perfection of Wisdom.

Likewise, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses faith and joy, possesses the practice of concentration, and possesses diligence, yet desires to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path but does not obtain the *prajñāpāramitā*, and fails to learn through transformative strategies and clear wisdom, they will midway attain the path of an *arhat* or a *pratyekabuddha*.

Those who possess faith and joy, practice meditative concentration, and exert diligence, desiring to attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment, and who succeed in learning the skillful wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*, shall never become weary midway; they will transcend the stages of the *arhat* and the *pratyekabuddha*, and shall be firmly established in the unsurpassed, true, and perfect enlightenment.
It is like a man or woman carrying an unbaked earthen jar to fetch water; they know it will surely break before long.
This is because it has not yet been fired.

Likewise, if one's learning does not reach this profound Dharma, one will ultimately be unable to attain all-knowledge (sarvajñatā); instead, one will become weary and turn back midway, falling into the two paths.
It is like carrying a clay jar while walking to fetch water; one returns home in safety.
Why is this? Because it has already been completed.
Having mastered the profound Dharma, one knows that it shall never end in mid-course, but will lead the mind at will toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way.

It is like a ship upon the great ocean: if it is not well guarded and one places worldly wealth and goods within it, when the voyage is ruined, those goods will be scattered and lost, and one’s precious treasures will perish.

Thus, even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva applies their mind with sincerity to study, if they do not attain the profound Dharma, you should know that they will become weary midway and lose the jewel of the name; through such mid-course indolence, they fall into the two paths.

It is like a person who repairs an old ship in the great ocean, places goods and wealth within it, and sets out for a destination; provided it does not sink midway, it will certainly reach its intended place.

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses faith and joy, the practice of meditative concentration, and diligent study, and further attains the profound Dharma, they never become lax midway; they stand firmly established in the supreme, unsurpassed, right, and true path, never falling into the two [lesser] paths, but proceeding directly toward the gate of the Buddha.
"It is like a person who is old and suffering from physical illness.
What do you think? Would such a person be able to rise from their bed by themselves?
Shan-yeh replied:
"No, O God among Gods!
At times he may arise, but lacking strength, he cannot move by himself; even if his illness should be cured and he is able to rise, he would still be unable to walk."
The Buddha said:

"In this way, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is equipped with the practices and studies as described above, yet fails to attain the profound Dharma while desiring to reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path, they will ultimately not become a Buddha; they will instead become weary midway and fall into the two paths."
It is, for example, like an old and sick person who has been cured and wishes to rise and walk; a strong man comes to support him and says to him:
"Do not fear; I shall escort you myself and will certainly not abandon you midway, but shall deliver you to the place you desire."

"In this way, a bodhisattva who possesses such superior conduct and has attained this profound *prajñāpāramitā* and transformative wisdom should know that they will never become weary midway; they will certainly be able to reach the ultimate goal and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
Chapter Thirteen: Analysis. The Bodhisattva Śukla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva train in the Perfection of Wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"One should associate with virtuous friends and follow the teachings of the Perfection of Wisdom with a benevolent mind.
What constitutes following these teachings? "

One should practice giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; do not become attached to the five aggregates.
Why is this? Because in the Perfection of Wisdom, omniscience is without attachment.
One must not take pleasure in the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"In this way, Kalyāṇamitra!
The Acalabodhisattva gradually enters into the Perfection of Wisdom.
Kalyāṇamitra said:
“Bodhisattvas undergo hardships, O God among Gods!
Those who wish to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path,” the Buddha said.
"Thus, through such humble austerity, he brings peace to the world; he is a protector for the ten directions, a refuge, a shelter, a crossing, a terrace, and a guide."
What is protection?
To protect all beings from the diligent toil of birth and death and to teach them deliverance—this is protection.
To deliver them entirely from birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is taking refuge.
"Having attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme enlightenment and having become a Tathāgata, one preaches the sūtras without attachment; this is 'dwelling.
He asked again:
'What is meant by "without attachment"? "
The Buddha said:

"The five aggregates are neither attached to nor bound; these five aggregates have no place from which they arise and no place to which they cease. This is why, when a bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, he becomes a shelter for the world."
What is it that a bodhisattva attains when they achieve the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme perfect enlightenment to deliver the world?
They deliver the five aggregates and yet are not the five aggregates; the five aggregates are themselves the deliverance, and deliverance is all dharmas.
Kalyāṇakarmā said:
“As the Buddha has taught, liberation is the nature of all dharmas, and through all sūtras one attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
For what reason?”
"Because they are without attachment.
The Buddha said:

"In this way, the bodhisattva who is without attachment endures hardships and remains diligent in mindfulness of the Dharma; he attains the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of supreme perfect enlightenment. It is for this reason that he preaches the sutras in such a manner to deliver the world."
What is the world-platform?
It is like a platform in water, which the water flows around on both sides.

In this way, the five aggregates (skandhas) are severed in the past, future, and present. When the five aggregates are severed, the training in all dharmas is also severed. This severance of all dharmas is concentration; it is the nectar; it is Nirvana.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the Dharma in this way, they then preach the Dharma; thus, when they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, they become a pedestal for the world.
What is the Way?
Thus, one fully realizes that the five aggregates and all phenomena, as described above, are empty; they have no origin from which they come and no trace to which they go, being like space.

They are without distinction or conceptualization, without location or consciousness, and have no source from which they arise; they are like dreams and illusions, boundless and without differentiation.
Kalyāṇakarmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is profound, O God among Gods!
Who would be able to fully comprehend this?”
The Buddha said:
"It has been a long time since they first sought Buddhahood before they finally came to believe.
Only those such as these can clearly understand the merits they cultivated during the time of past Buddhas."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'having sought Buddhahood for a long time'?
The Buddha said:
"Since one has departed from and transcended the five aggregates, they no longer exist; this is what clarifies this profound Dharma.
Such a bodhisattva acts for the sake of immeasurable people on the path."
Kalyāṇakarmā said,
“He is a guide for those among men.
The Buddha said:
"Indeed! When a bodhisattva attains such practice as described above, they become a guide for immeasurable people; this constitutes a great covenant, a vow made for immeasurable beings."

Not bound by the five aggregates, not bound by those who follow the path of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha, not abandoning all-knowledge, and not bound by any phenomena—therefore, this is the oath.
Kalyāṇakārin said:
“The bodhisattva seeking the profound perfection of wisdom does not cherish the three states—the state of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or even that of a buddha.
“It is most profound, O God among Gods!”
There is neither one who guards nor one who does not guard.

That which is "not non-guarding" arises from within the Perfection of Wisdom as the dharma of non-emergence; it is guarding concentration, guarding the non-guarding of all dharmas, guarding non-existence, guarding the infinite, and guarding non-attachment.
The Buddha said:
"One who practices in this manner within the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) shall likewise be non-retrogressive.
A bodhisattva, having no attachment within the Perfection of Wisdom, never follows the words of ordinary people, does not believe in other paths, and is neither terrified, nor afraid, nor indolent."
"You should know this: that person has already received this illumination from the Buddhas of the past.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If a bodhisattva is neither terrified nor afraid, and is not indolent, for what reason should they contemplate and observe within the Perfection of Wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"To direct the mind toward all-knowledge is what constitutes contemplation.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is meant by directing the mind toward all-knowledge?"
The Buddha said:
"When the mind inclines toward emptiness, this is contemplation.
Not viewing that which is incalculable—wherein all-knowledge is like the incalculable—is what constitutes the non-existence of the five aggregates."

It does not enter, it is not attained, and it is not known; there is neither knowing nor non-knowing. It has no arising and no destruction, no agent, no point of origin, and no trace of departure. It is neither seen nor located; just as such space is immeasurable, so too is all-knowledge (sarvajñā) incalculable.
"There is no Buddha who acts, and no Buddha who attains; there is no Buddha attained from within the five aggregates, nor is there a Buddha attained through the six perfections.
The Devaputra of Desire and the Devaputra of Brahma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Profound, O God among Gods!"
"It is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
The Buddha said to the devaputras:
"Such is the vision of the Tathāgata; such is his peace and profound depth."
"It is known that one who fully knows this possesses non-retrogression toward unsurpassed, most perfect enlightenment, yet there is no such thing as 'most perfect enlightenment'.
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare indeed for those who believe in this sutra; you have spoken it out of compassion for the world."
"Whatever people of the world desire, they are all attached to.
The Buddha said: "It is so."
Chapter 14: On Original Non-existence. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“All dharmas are, in their successive order, without attachment; they are without conceptualization, like empty space. This sutra has no point of origin; when one searches for all dharmas, nothing can be found.”
The devaputra of Desire and the devaputra of Brahmā said:
"This is the work of wholesome karma; as the Tathāgata has taught, one should simply speak of the wisdom of space.
The devaputra of Wholesome Karma replied:
“The Tathāgata follows the teaching of the Tathāgata.
What is meant by ‘following the teaching’?
That which is non-arising according to the Dharma is following the teaching; this is primordial non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*), having neither a point of origin nor a trace of departure.”
All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, and the Tathāgata is likewise fundamentally non-existent and no different.
To follow this fundamental non-existence is to follow the fundamental non-existence of the Tathāgata.
The establishment of the Tathāgata’s fundamental non-existence constitutes following the teaching of the Tathāgata.
It is not different from all phenomena; there is no difference, for it is fundamentally non-existent.
There is no agent; all things are fundamentally non-existent, and even that fundamental non-existence is itself non-existent, being equal and without distinction.

Within the true Dharma, there is fundamentally nothing; all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, lacking past, future, or present. The Tathāgata is likewise so; this is what is meant by "true fundamental non-existence."

When the bodhisattvas attain the name of "Tathāgata of Original Non-existence," the earth shakes in six ways; this is what the Tathāgata calls "Original Non-existence," and it is the good karma of his disciples that follows the Tathāgata’s teaching.
"Furthermore, the five aggregates, the srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, the anāgāmin, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha do not receive [anything]; this is called 'following the teaching.
Śāriputra said to the Buddha, "The ultimate non-arising (anupapatti) is profoundly deep, O God among Gods!"

When this teaching on original non-existence was being expounded, two hundred bhikṣus attained the stage of a śrotāpanna; five hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the path of a srota-āpanna; five hundred devas and humans all attained the joy of the dharma of non-arising and stood therein; and sixty newly initiated bodhisattvas attained the path of a śrotāpanna.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"In past lives, these sixty people each made offerings to five hundred Buddhas; they all practiced giving, upheld the precepts, cultivated patience, exerted diligence, and attained meditative concentration, yet they did not understand emptiness."

Although they have attained emptiness, because they do not obtain the protection of the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and the transformative wisdom of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), they now all fall into the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

If a Bodhisattva possesses the Way and attains emptiness, signlessness (animitta), and wishlessness (apraṇihita), yet does not obtain the Perfection of Wisdom and the transformative wisdom of skillful means, they will then fall midway into those two paths.

"It is as if there were a great bird, its body twenty thousand *li* in length, which, being without wings, threw itself down from the heavens; if it wished to turn back midway, would it be able to do so?
He replied, "It could not."
“When one has reached the ground, if one wishes for the body not to feel pain, can it truly avoid feeling pain?
He replied, “It cannot.”
Some fainted, while others died. Why was this?
Because their bodies were large and they had no wings.

Even if a bodhisattva were to practice giving, uphold the precepts, practice patience, exert diligence, and seek the meditative concentrations of form for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, yet does not enter into emptiness and does not enter into the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and fails to attain transformative skillful means and clear insight—though their mind greatly resolves to seek the Buddha-way and they desire to become a Buddha in every respect—they will instead midway attain the stage of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.

If one practices before the Buddha as described above, yet hears of the Buddha’s omniscience and thinks of seeking it as if it were a physical form, this constitutes not upholding the Tathāgata’s morality, concentration, and wisdom, and failing to understand omniscience. Merely hearing the sound of its characteristics—like hearing with the ears—one then attempts to achieve unsurpassed, equal, and most perfect enlightenment; one will certainly be unable to attain it and will instead fall midway.
"Why is this? Because they have not attained the profound Dharma.
Kauṣṭhila addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught, if a bodhisattva, while contemplating, becomes detached from the profound Dharma, they will instead attain the stage of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.
If one truly desires to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme perfect enlightenment, one must study the Prajñāpāramitā and cultivate transformative wisdom."
The Devaputra of Desire and the Devaputra of Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is difficult to understand the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Śubhakṛtsna said:
“It is difficult to comprehend, O God among Gods!
According to my reflection on this wisdom, the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path is easily attained. Why is this?
Since there is nothing, how could one attain Buddhahood? Why is this?
All phenomena are empty; though one searches for phenomena, they cannot be found.
"One who would become a Buddha seeks the Dharma but finds nothing to be obtained;
thus, seeking Buddhahood is easily attained. Kauṣṭhila said:
"What has been spoken is difficult to attain. Why is this?
Emptiness does not conceive the thought, 'I shall become a Buddha.'"
"This Dharma is like empty space; if it were easy to attain, why would all the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have already reached it?
He replied, "How so?
Is it attained by means of the five aggregates?"
He replied, “No.
[The Buddha asked:
“Does one attain it by being apart from the five aggregates?”
"No. "How so? Śāriputra asked. Śāradvatīputra replied:
"The five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent;
can one then attain them? He replied, "No."
“Is there a dharma that can be attained apart from these? He replied, “No.”
“How is it? Can this ‘original non-existence’ (mūlābhāva) bring about attainment? He replied, “No.”
“Is there a method to attain it by departing from them? He replied, “No.”
"Since these dharmas cannot be attained, what dharma could there be that brings about attainment?
Śāriputra said: "As you have explained, O Great Being, those who travel in equanimity do not attain anything at all."
The Buddha taught that those who possess the three kinds of merit seek the path of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha.
Yet, they do not conceive of these three as being three; rather, they seek them for the sake of the One Path.
"Just as Kalyāṇakārin has said.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāradvatīputra, "Kalyāṇakārin speaks of a single path; you should question him about it."
Śāriputra said:
"I ask this because you have spoken of the One Way.
He replied:
“How is it that one perceives the three paths within primordial non-existence?
He replied,
“I do not perceive them.”
"Why is this? Because within that which is fundamentally non-existent, these three things cannot be found.
Shan-ye said:
"Is there not even a single thing that can be attained? He replied, "No."
“Can one attain the One Path within primordial non-existence? He replied, “No.”
Kalyāṇakarma said:
"If even this Truth is unattainable, for what reason do you further speak of the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas?

As the Way is taught, it is fundamentally non-existent and without distinction; one who hears of this fundamental non-existence and does not become indolent will surely attain supreme, perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha said:
“It is as you have said, without difference. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I shall cause you to speak of the fundamental non-arising as being equal and without difference.
Kauṣṭhila asked:
"What is awakening?
The Buddha said,
"It is the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Kalyāṇakarmā asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes the accomplishment of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha said:
“Treat all people with impartiality, bestow compassion and pity upon them, and do not harbor anger.
Standing thus, you should train yourself in this way.
Chapter Fifteen: Non-Retrogression. Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"How should one compare and observe the conduct and characteristics of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva so as to recognize them?
The Buddha said:

"It is like one who has attained dhyāna, being unmoving and unshakable; it is like the stage of Pratyekabuddha, like the stage of a Buddha, and like *bhūtatathatā* (suchness), which is fundamentally and eternally unmoving."
The Buddha taught that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*).

Those who hear this do not say it is not like the fundamental non-existence of space; they recognize that fundamental non-existence is the true nature of all things, and just as with fundamental non-existence itself, they do not deny it.
Having heard thus, even if they subsequently hear it elsewhere, they never doubt it nor speak of its being right or wrong.
As it was originally established, their words are sincere and weighty; they do not speak of unprincipled ordinary people, nor do they observe the perverse deeds of those who oppose the Way.
By means of these signs and modes of conduct, one knows with certainty that this is a non-retrogressive Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, one does not judge a śramaṇa or brahmin by their physical appearance or facial features.

Discerning them through the truth and seeing them through the truth, one never offers words of praise, nor prostrates, nor presents flowers and incense to the gods, nor does one instruct others to do so.
By means of these signs and practices being fully perfected, one knows this;
furthermore, one will never again be born in an evil realm, nor will one take birth as a woman, for by means of these signs and practices being fully perfected, one knows this.

Furthermore, the non-retrogressive Mahāsattva upholds the precepts: he himself does not kill and teaches others not to kill; he himself does not steal and teaches others not to steal; he himself does not engage in sexual misconduct and teaches others not to engage in sexual misconduct; he himself does not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, or frivolous chatter, nor in envy, malice, or delusion. He teaches others likewise not to do so.

One personally upholds these ten precepts and further teaches others to observe and practice them; one protects the ten precepts even in dreams and perceives them face-to-face. By means of such signs and characteristics, one knows that their conduct is fully perfected.

Furthermore, one studies all dharmas; using this mind, one studies these dharmas and preaches the sutras for the sake of bringing peace and stability to all living beings. Upholding this sutra, one receives and distributes its merit, vowing that all beings may attain this pure concentration (*samādhi*) so as to establish themselves in clarity. Through these corresponding signs and practices, one attains complete knowledge.
Furthermore, when the Great Being preaches the profound Dharma, he never doubts, never speaks with lack of faith, nor does he feel fear; his speech is gentle and beautiful.
He sleeps little, and his walking and movement are orderly; his entrance and exit are unhurried, his mind proceeds slowly and with composure, and he walks while carefully discerning the ground.
His clothing is always pure within; it is free from fleas, lice, dust, and grime, and he has no anxiety. Within his body there are none of the eighty kinds of worms. Why is this so?

"The merit of the six perfections of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas surpasses that of the worthies and sages; as they gradually seek to bring them to fulfillment, their bodies and minds become pure and clean, and they fully realize their lofty aspirations.
Suyīn (Good Deeds) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is this so, O God among Gods?"
“How is it that the mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is pure and clean?
The Buddha said:

“As the merit they have performed increases and progresses further upward, their minds are without obstruction and they fully attain all merit; this purity of mind surpasses that of those who correspond to the stage of *śrāvaka* and those who are *pratyekabuddhas*. By means of these signs and practices, one knows them to be fully endowed.”
Furthermore, when others come to offer gifts or leave behind offerings, he does not give rise to joy.
He is entirely free from stinginess; regarding the exposition of profound sutras, he never experiences weariness, and he enters deeply into wisdom.
If there are others who wish to hear the sutras elsewhere, one should take up this Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) and expound it for them.
If there are those in other paths who are not upright, one should take up the Perfection of Wisdom and rectify them.

The dharmas set forth in the sūtras all speak of the matter of impermanence; that which cannot be understood through the worldly scriptures is explained by means of this Prajñāpāramitā, through which one comes to possess complete knowledge of these characteristics and practices.
This wicked Māra gradually approaches their location and, manifesting eight great hells at their side, points to the bodhisattvas therein and says:
"These people have all received the prediction of non-retrogression from previous Buddhas."
Now they have all fallen into hell.
The Buddha bestows [the precepts] upon them, even if they are in hell.
If they should quickly repent and say:
"I am not one who has regressed from non-retrogression.
If one speaks thus, they shall no longer enter the hells and will instead be reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said:
"If this mind remains unmoved, know that he is non-retrogressive; know him by his being fully endowed with these marks and practices.
Furthermore, Māra may manifest as a teacher, dressed in robes, and go to where he is, saying:
'Whatever you previously heard from me, all that which was received—discard it entirely; none of it is to be used.'"
"If you repent quickly and follow my words, I shall come daily to inquire after your well-being.
If you do not heed my words, I will never come again.
Do not speak of this matter anymore; I have no desire to hear it."
"What was previously said were merely external matters; listen further to my words, for these are what the Buddha has taught. The Buddha said:

"If, upon hearing this, one should waver or change their mind, you should know that such a person did not receive the prediction of enlightenment from a past Buddha, nor have they ascended into the stage of non-retrogression among the Great Beings."
Even if one remains unmoved and contemplates this sutra, it is brought about by emptiness; reflecting thus, one does not believe in false words.

For example, just as a bhikṣu who has attained the stage of Arhat does not accept false words, having seen the scriptural evidence with his own eyes, he realizes it is brought about by emptiness and can never be moved.
Just as the dharmas contemplated by those of proper deportment and the pratyekabuddhas never again regress, so it is for this Great Being who is heading toward Buddhahood.
Standing firmly upon the stage of non-retrogression, he has reached the ultimate limit; one knows this through the perfection of these signs and practices.
The evil Mara went again to where he was and, appearing in the guise of another person, said:
"That which you seek is merely the pursuit of suffering; it is not the seeking of the Buddha-dharma."

If one carries such difficulties as these while seeking [liberation], and remains in the evil realms for many long ages, even if one should eventually obtain human form, would one not reflect upon this and feel weary of one's own suffering?
"Where else could one seek such a body?
Why not take up the state of an Arhat sooner, rather than seeking to become a Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"If he does not turn back, the evil one will again depart.
He will employ further skillful means, manifesting as several bodhisattvas standing by his side, and go to point them out, saying:

'If you see these bodhisattvas, you should all make offerings to them—robes, food, bedding, and medicine—as if to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; you should fully receive their teachings and inquire about wisdom; you should learn everything they practice and seek; you should abide according to the Dharma and seek according to the Dharma; if you enter into this and perform such studies and practices, you shall never attain Buddhahood.'"
"Can you obtain it through conditions?
The Buddha said:
"If one is not moved by this, they will not stray far from the truth. [The Māra] then manifests as a group of bhikṣus and says:"
“‘If those Arhats of past ages all sought the path of a bodhisattva, yet having already attained Arhatship, how could they have subsequently become Buddhas?
The Buddha said:

‘For this reason, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, hearing it from another, his mind does not waver or change; he further recognizes within this that what is spoken by the Buddha is no different [from the truth], and thus seeks the Great Illumination and plants his resolve.’”
If this were so, and one did not attain Buddhahood, then the Buddha’s words would be erroneous.
Since the Buddha’s words are never deceptive, you should train in this way and seek in this way; guard this teaching with truth so that the mind does not waver, and therein awaken to what is false.
By means of these signs and practices, one knows with certainty that this is non-retrogression.
Furthermore, a malicious and harassing person may say:
"The Buddha is like space; this sūtra-practice is boundless and its limit cannot be attained."

Why is this? The meaning of this sutra can be understood: observe that all destinations are but emptiness; for those who exert themselves in toil and suffering are improper, as they perceive these things as perverse and act perversely—this is merely the sutra.
"How can one wish to become a Buddha?
This is not what the Buddha has taught. The Buddha said:
“Now, worthy men and women possess clear vision and far-reaching deliberation; they examine themselves with discernment, thinking:
‘The wicked and the heterodox abound in cleverness, taking the perverse as the compliant.
Yet when strange things come, we do not waver, remaining as firm as Mount Sumeru.’”
"By means of these signs and practices being fully perfected, one knows this is non-retrogression.

One may practice the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; yet while remaining in these concentrations, one does not cling to them as the dhyānas themselves. Because one employs these concentrations to enter into the realm of desire, the non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva does not follow the teachings of concentration, but remains pure beyond the states of concentration. By means of these signs and practices being fully perfected, one knows this."
Furthermore, when others praise his name and virtues, he does not feel joy; his mind remains undisturbed and he always maintains a correct mind.
Even if he lives at home, he does not indulge in excessive lust. Should desire arise at times, it is like being in a vast, desolate wilderness while eating and drinking:
terrified and fearing bandits, one wishes to depart quickly, thinking to oneself, "When shall I emerge from this empty wilderness?"
One should form this thought: "I am mindful that a woman’s impure menses are not my pure dharma. Why is this?
"It is because he intends to bring peace and security to the people of the ten directions.

The Dharma they know cannot be matched by those of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or any gods, humans, ghosts, dragons, yakṣas, or spirits.”
