The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śubhakārin: "In dreams, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not enter the stage of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha, nor does he teach others to enter therein."
To view all phenomena as if in a dream, with the mind and will always fixed upon the Buddha—know that this is the mark of non-retrogression.

To sit together with hundreds of thousands of disciples in a dream, preaching the sutras, and to be at the very forefront accompanied by a multitude of *bhikṣus* (those who have removed their hunger), such that the Tathāgata sees them all preaching the sutras—this is the mark of a bodhisattva who has attained non-retrogression.

In a dream, he sat in mid-air and preached the sutras for the various *bhikṣus*; he further saw a seven-foot radiance emanating from himself, as he performed transformations at other locations with sovereign ease, just as a Buddha preaches the sutras.
In dreams, they feel no fear, no terror, and no dread of hardships.

Even if they see prefectures and counties where armies have risen and are attacking one another, or witness calamities of fire and water, the harm of tigers, wolves, lions, and venomous insects, or see the decapitation of people—regarding all such other transformations, as well as those who are afflicted by toil, poverty, hunger, and thirst—they behold all these misfortunes and their minds remain unafraid.
Upon waking, he immediately rises from his seat and reflects:
"Just as I saw these three places in my dream, when I become a Buddha, I shall preach the sutras and teach them everywhere.
One should know that this is the mark of non-retrogression.
How is this known?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains Buddhahood, there shall be no evil whatsoever within his realm.
At that very time, if one were to see in a dream animals preying upon one another or the people suffering from epidemics, [it would indicate otherwise].
His mind gradually gave rise to the thought:
"May there be no evil whatsoever within my realm.
It is by this that it is known.
Having awakened from a dream, if one sees a city or fortress on fire, one should think:
"Such a sign can indeed be seen within a dream.
Seeing it without fear, and acting with the full perfection of such signs, this is a bodhisattva who is non-retrogressive.
“If it is now truly as I have discerned—that this is what I am destined for—then there shall be no such extraordinary transformation.
The fire that has arisen shall be extinguished; it shall be entirely consumed and vanish so that it is seen no more.
The Buddha said:
"If the fire were to be extinguished immediately, I would know that I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from a past Buddha.
If the fire were not to be extinguished, I would know that I have not yet received the prediction.
Suppose the Fire God burns one house and spares another."
Again, he caused a fire to arise that burned one *li* and then ceased at another *li*.
He knew this was caused by his family members having interrupted the sūtras in a previous life.
For such people, all their deeds become clearly visible; thus, the evil they committed in past lives is entirely eliminated.

From this point onward, the remaining karmic retributions for past transgressions will be severed and completely exhausted; yet one should know that they have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Using this perspective and maintaining these signs, you should explain it to others so that they may understand it.
At times, when men or women are possessed by spirits, they may have this thought:

"Now that I have received the prediction—having been granted the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment by a Tathāgata of the past—my thoughts are entirely pure; having set aside the minds of those who attain the stage of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, I shall surely become a Buddha."
Among all the Buddhas currently existing in the ten directions, there are none who do not know and witness this.
Now the Tathāgata fully knows the deliberations and thoughts within me; it is because of me that these spirits and deities are departing.
"One who does not go has not yet received the prediction.
The Buddha said:
"If that person is truly sincere, Māra the Evil One will come before them and say:"
"If you originally made this dwelling and were originally named so-and-so when you received the prediction," they said,
wishing to confuse him with these words.
The bodhisattva replied:
"I have truly received my prediction [of enlightenment]; the spirits and deities must now depart.
The malevolent deity thought to himself:
"I shall cause the ghosts to leave."
The ghost then departed.
This was because the celestial deity was most honored and possessed majestic spiritual power, which the ghost did not dare to confront.
The bodhisattva reflected in turn:
"It is only because of my majestic spiritual power that they have departed.
Thereupon, he became arrogant, looked down upon the worthy ones, and showed them no respect or deference,
saying:
"Having already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Tathāgatas of the past," he becomes arrogant;
instead of rising [in virtue], he gives rise to anger and further conceives sinful thoughts, and shall consequently fall into two paths.
One should be aware that taking what is unaccomplished as accomplished is a perverse practice;
one should be aware of this matter when abandoning virtuous friends and becoming entangled by the perverse.

The perverse ones repeatedly go back and forth, speaking of past instances of receiving predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and even displaying the family names and lineages of one's parents and relatives for seven generations.
If one was born in a certain kingdom, district, or village and now speaks these gentle words, it is because they also spoke such gentle words in previous lives.
Furthermore, he says:
"If one has already received the prediction of enlightenment, they shall attain non-retrogression."
Upon hearing this, the man was filled with great joy and, convinced it was indeed so, he began to behave with arrogance and disdain toward his fellow students.

Because of these words, he lost his original practice and fell into the net of evil; by accepting those words, he failed to perceive his own depravity and claimed to have attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
The evil one spoke again, saying:
"When you become a Buddha, your name shall be such-and-such.
Upon hearing this name, he thought to himself:
"Is it not so that I have attained this?
From my birth, I have inherently possessed this aspiration.
The Buddha said:
"Among those bodhisattvas, there are some who possess little wisdom of adaptive strategy; instead, they give rise to this thought:
'If it were created by wicked deities, then these *pudgalas* would be deluded by them.'"
The Buddha said:

“Those bodhisattvas whom I have designated do not teach them to form such thoughts, for doing so distances one from all-knowledge, causes one to lose the virtue of skillful means and depart from the Great Illumination, and leads one to abandon virtuous friends while placing faith in the wicked and foolish.”
These people will eventually fall into two paths; if they undergo diligent suffering for a long time in the future, they will then seek Buddhahood again.
By virtue of the grace of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they shall themselves attain the state of a Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“At that time, when one gives rise to such a thought and accepts this title, if one does not immediately realize it and repent, one shall thus fall into two paths.

If there is a *pudgala* who has received the heavy prohibitions of the four rules, or if they commit another offense and violate these prohibitions, they do not become a śramaṇa and are not a son of the Buddha.”
When a bodhisattva says,
"I was born in such-and-such a country, district, county,
or village," at the moment they form this thought of birth, their transgression regarding the four requisites for sustenance is the most grave.
Setting aside these four grave matters, there are the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
One should give rise to this thought in one's mind, receive its literal meaning, and believe it; the retribution for such a crime is exceedingly heavy.
One should understand it in this way.
Because of using these words, one incurs the grave sin of entering into perversion.
The perverse one further utters these words:
"The distancing from dharmas is precisely as it should be, as proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One."
The Buddha said to Shan-ye:
"I do not speak of 'seclusion' in this way when I instruct bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to dwell in the quietude between trees.
Shan-ye replied:
“How is it, O God among Gods!
What further distinctions are there in seclusion?
The Buddha said:

"Furthermore, let each of them follow this practice of mindfulness appropriate to their station; let those who aspire to the stage of a Pratyekabuddha follow this practice of mindfulness; and let each Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice seclusion outside the city, so that no evil whatsoever may be committed."
If one should dwell in seclusion among the trees in solitary places, one will fully comprehend the dharma of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
I delight in having them practice in this way, rather than sending them far away to dwell in desolate, uninhabited regions.
One should practice this seclusion with diligence day and night; therefore it is said:
"One who practices seclusion should do so near a city.
Such is the Dharma I have taught.
At that time, Māra the Evil One shall go to instruct him in the practice of seclusion, saying to him:
"If you are to dwell alone in the midst of trees, you should practice in this manner."
"Following false teachings, one then loses the dharma of detachment.
As for the words of such heterodox speech, the Way is the same; there is no difference between those who follow the proper rites and those who are pratyekabuddhas."
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva has not yet attained his aspirations, yet he acts contrary to them.
He has not yet mastered the Dharma, yet he obstinately regards himself as superior and treats other bodhisattvas with contempt, becoming arrogant and thinking, 'Who can surpass me?'"

Dwelling near the light city, with a mind clear and pure in its reflections, they do not enter the stages of the Śrāvakas or abide within the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas; they do not accept any evil, and having cast off meditative absorptions through detachment, they regain them within concentration, fully fulfilling all their vows and crossing over to liberation.
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva lacks transformative strategy and clear wisdom, even if they dwell for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years—or even longer—in a desolate wilderness where neither birds, beasts, nor rākṣasas can reach, yet remain ignorant of the dharma of detachment, it will ultimately be of no benefit."
Māra then flew up into the air and stood there, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! This is the true dharma of seclusion spoken by the Tathāgata.
You should indeed practice this seclusion accordingly, and you will swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."

Upon hearing this, the man was delighted; he immediately rose and went to the outskirts of the city. Having distanced himself from those who had achieved virtue and noble conduct, he instead spoke with contempt, saying:
"The Dharma you practice is not correct."
The Buddha said:

"Among such practitioners, there are those who practice correctly yet call it wrong, and those who act perversely yet call it right; they show reverence to those who do not deserve it, and treat with anger and arrogance those whom they ought to revere."
The Bodhisattva of False Speech said:
"I am practicing seclusion.
A flying person came and spoke to me, saying:"
“Excellent, excellent!
This is indeed the Dharma of seclusion; you should truly practice in accordance with it, for this reason I have come to speak to you.
If you were practicing near a city, who would have come to speak to you?”
The Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva possesses virtue yet treats others with such contempt, you should understand it thus:
he is like one who carries a corpse; having no worth whatsoever, he instead calls out the faults of this bodhisattva. Such a person is an enemy to the bodhisattva."
One who detests the noble conduct of a bodhisattva is a great thief among gods and men.
Even if such a person wears the robes of a śramaṇa and dwells among the ranks of bodhisattvas, they are nonetheless a thief; one must not associate with them, nor engage in conversation or laughter.
Why is this? Because excessive anger and resentment destroy a person's good intentions.
One should understand it thus.

One should always firmly uphold the Dharma that is to be protected; one should purify the mind and establish the mind upon what is wholesome; one should practice with diligent retention and always maintain a correct mind even in places of fear and arduous suffering.
One must not enter the three places where those who possess broken vessels dwell.
One should always maintain a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, seeking to bring them peace and security, feeling pity for them, and guarding one's own thoughts:
"May I never give rise to defiled, turbid, or evil thoughts; should any unwholesome states arise within me, may I quickly abandon them."
"This is the supreme practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;
it should be understood in this way.
Chapter Nineteen: On Good Friends "Furthermore, Śubhakarma! "

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are resolute in their great aspiration and desire to attain the unsurpassed, right, true path of supreme perfect enlightenment should attend upon virtuous friends and revere the Three Honored Ones.
Kalyāṇakarmā asked:
"How, O Good Friend, should one know this?
The Buddha said:
"If there is a person who explains the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) and teaches others to enter this samādhi, such a person is a good friend to the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

The six perfections are good friends; they are virtuous qualities, protection, leadership, and deliverance. The Tathāgata of supreme perfect enlightenment, as well as all the Tathāgatas in the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions in the past, future, and present, have all attained the path of omniscience through wisdom and protect sentient beings by means of four matters."
What are the four?
First, giving; second, encouraging others to find joy [in giving]; third, benefiting others; and fourth, giving equally.
These are the four virtues.
They act as parents, as a home, as a terrace, as a means of crossing over, as a refuge, and as a guide; therefore, the six perfections serve as the means of deliverance for sentient beings.

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas study the six perfections, they do so for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to sever their roots entirely; thus they study the characteristics of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
What, then, are these characteristics of the perfection of wisdom?
"The characteristic of the unimpeded perfection of wisdom is that this characteristic is the attainment of all dharmas.
The Buddha said, "In this way, there is no characteristic by which one attains the perfection of wisdom; it is through this very characteristic that one attains all dharmas."
"Why is this? All dharmas are each empty, and these marks are also empty; this is called the Perfection of Wisdom.
Subhūti asked the Buddha:
"Furthermore, O God among Gods!
Since all dharmas are each empty, for what reason do sentient beings desire birth when there is no time of cessation?
Emptiness does not increase, nor does it ever rest; each is like space, formless."
The unsurpassed, perfect, true path of supreme, right enlightenment does not arise from within this;
each being is empty, and one cannot attain the unsurpassed, perfect, true path of supreme, right enlightenment [therein].
"How so, O God among Gods!
By what means should this Dharma be known with certainty?
The Buddha said:
"All you sentient beings, through diligent toil and longing, desire to obtain this cause and bring about this result; thus do you seek it.
Do you see that I have attained emptiness?
Shan-ye replied:
"No, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"One creates this and obtains this; is this empty?"
He replied,
"It is like space, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said:
"But for this reason alone, would there be no time of liberation?
He replied,
"It is so, O God among Gods!"
"Though people desire such supreme peace and security, they strive for it without ceasing through toil and hardship.
The Buddha said:
"It is because of what people desire that they become attached."
One should understand it thus:

that which is born among the people fundamentally arises from this state of non-apprehension; that which is non-apprehended does not constitute a "non-existence," and in this non-existence, at the time of cessation, there is neither arising nor increase.
"By understanding in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Does the bodhisattva seek to understand in this way because he does not seek the five aggregates?"
Is it for the sake of seeking the Perfection of Wisdom? Or is it for the sake of seeking them all equally?
These are beyond the reach of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

A person of virtue who seeks the lofty Way, such that none can equal them, should practice in this manner, swiftly drawing near day and night to the unsurpassed, truly correct Way of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment.
The Buddha said:

"Suppose all the sentient beings of the four continents were to become human, and each were to seek the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, resolve their minds to seek the Buddha-way, and throughout their entire lives practice giving for the sake of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."
“What do you think, Subhūti? Would the merit from such wholesome karma be great?
He replied, “It would be very great, O World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"If one attains the pure concentration of the Perfection of Wisdom and maintains it for even a single day, practicing according to the instructions herein and forming such thoughts and actions, this merit exceeds that [previous merit]. Why is this? Because..."
No sentient beings' conduct can equal this loving-kindness.

This noble person has deeply entered into wisdom and fully understands that this wisdom is complete; seeing the toil and suffering of the world, they immediately give rise to universal compassion and take pity on all. With the eye of the Way, they clearly perceive all living beings, achieving and perfecting their lofty resolve, acting without indolence.
It is through unflagging diligence that they attain this.

Those bodhisattvas extend their great compassion universally; they do not abide by these marks, nor do they abide by anything else. Their wisdom is brilliantly luminous, and although they have not yet fully established themselves in the unsurpassed, right, and true path, they are honored throughout all buddha-fields. They uphold the supreme, true path and shall never turn back.

If one receives offerings of clothing, food, bedding, and medicine, one should remain established within this mind of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Whatever gifts are received should be set aside for the sake of attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); what is consumed shall be without fault. One benefits sentient beings by fully demonstrating the abiding of the Way, illuminating them to their boundless limits. Those who are in prisons are all delivered and liberated; one demonstrates the eye of the Way to them—following this practice, do not dwell on signs, do not harbor divergent thoughts or hold onto faults, and enter the high practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* without indolence.
It is like having obtained a bright moon jewel and then losing it;
one sits in great sorrow and distress, giving rise to anxious thoughts.
It is as if one had lost the seven treasures, and one thinks:
"How have I lost this treasure?
Those who wish to seek out precious jewels should always maintain their resolve firmly, so as not to lose the attainment of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Why is this?
"The Perfection of Wisdom is like empty space; it neither increases nor decreases.
Shan-ye said, "Regarding empty space, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplish their practice and draw near to the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
The Buddha said:
“The bodhisattva mahāsattva neither increases nor decreases.
When this is spoken in the sutras, they hear it without fear or dread.”
"You should know that such a person of high caliber is one who seeks the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Śubhakarṣa asked,
"Is this Perfection of Wisdom sought as emptiness?"
The Buddha said: "No.
[The interlocutor asked:
"Is there a way to attain it apart from the Perfection of Wisdom?"
The Buddha said, “No. Śubhakārin asked:
"Is it sought by means of the five aggregates?
The Buddha said, "No."
He asked again:
"Apart from the five aggregates, is there anything to be sought?
The Buddha said:
"No," said Shan-ye, "how does one seek the Great Illumination?"
The Buddha said:
"If one perceives these dharmas in this way, what dharma would there be to seek in the Perfection of Wisdom?
He replied:
“I do not see it, O God among Gods!
The Buddha said: “How so?
One who perceives this Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) everywhere—what kind of bodhisattva seeks it?”
He replied, "I did not see him.
The Buddha said:
"If one were to see everywhere, would there be any place where dharmas arise?
He replied, "I do not see any."
The Buddha said:

"These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall again attain the joy of the dharma of non-arising; they will be fully endowed with the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme perfect enlightenment, which is free from all reception of [phenomena]. Wherever they go, they shall have no further fear. They shall practice this protection, this seeking, this conduct, and this power, in order to return to the Buddha-wisdom, the ultimate great wisdom, the sovereign wisdom, the all-encompassing wisdom, and the Tathāgata-wisdom."
"If one acts in this way, one will not attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha said,
"There is a difference."
Kalyāṇakarmā asked:
“If all dharmas are non-arising, can one receive the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
"No," said Kṣemadatta. "How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path?"
The Buddha asked,
"Do you see those who are destined to receive their prediction [of enlightenment]?
They replied:
"One should not perceive dharmas when attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The Buddha said: "It is so!"
All dharmas cannot be obtained from within.
A bodhisattva does not form this thought:
"By means of these dharmas, I shall receive the prediction of enlightenment, or I shall not receive the prediction."
20. Chapter on Śakra Devānām Indra. Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha amidst the assembly, saying:
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to fathom and difficult to know."
"The merit of devas and humans is great when they encounter the teaching of this samādhi.
Those who hear it, write it down, uphold it, and study it possess exceedingly great merit.
Thus the Buddha spoke to Śakra.

"Even if all the people of Jambudvīpa were to uphold the ten precepts and maintain them in their entirety, the merit of this would not equal even a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part of that of a virtuous person who hears, upholds, and studies the Prajñāpāramitā sūtra."
At that time, there was a śrāvaka in the assembly who said to the Śākyas,
"He has already passed you all.
They replied:
“Holding this mind for even a single thought surpasses me; how much more so those who write it down, uphold it, study it, follow these teachings of the Dharma, and establish themselves therein.
Their brilliant virtue exceeds that of all beings within the three realms, and it further surpasses those at the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.”

When a bodhisattva practices the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditation, if they further attain the perfection of wisdom and the transformative insight of clear intelligence, they likewise surpass those [other perfections].

When the bodhisattva-mahāsattva seeks the Perfection of Wisdom and practices the Middle Way with familiarity, gods, humans, ghosts, and dragons—even those harboring venomous malice—can never overcome them.
By maintaining such firm resolve, they swiftly approach all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) and do not depart from the Tathāgata; this is called being "not far from the Buddha’s seat."
Do not give rise to indolence; train for the sake of Buddhahood, and do not train in the dharmas of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
The Four Heavenly Kings shall go to inquire after you.
Train diligently as a disciple of the fourfold assembly; you shall attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path upon the seat of the Buddha—thus should you train.
"The Four Heavenly Kings constantly go themselves to inquire after his well-being, let alone other sons of gods.
Ānanda had this thought:
"Is this Śakra speaking from his own wisdom?"
"Is it by holding the Buddha's majestic spiritual power?
The Buddha, knowing what Ānanda was thinking in his mind, said to Ānanda:
"It is by holding the Buddha's majestic spiritual power."
The Buddha said:

"In this regard, Ānanda, there may be times when a bodhisattva mahāsattva deeply contemplates and seeks to study the Prajñāpāramitā; then all the demons within the three thousandfold world-system will become distressed and poisonous, desiring to collectively disrupt and confuse him so that he might attain realization midway."
Chapter 21: On Arrogance. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The bodhisattvas, at all times, each study the *prajñāpāramitā* and practice it in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, throughout the various Buddha-fields, those who followed the ways of heterodoxy were each struck with alarm and thought:
"May my bodhisattvas attain the stage of Arhat midway through their practice; let them not attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment."

When Māra, the Evil One, sees a bodhisattva practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, he becomes deeply distressed and tormented; he sets fires on all four sides to terrify the bodhisattvas, intending to cause their resolve to waver.
The Buddha said:
"Māra does not personally travel everywhere to cause confusion.
However, if a bodhisattva distances himself from a virtuous teacher, he will be confused and afflicted by grief by Māra."
Because they do not deeply understand the Perfection of Wisdom, their minds are filled with doubt and they think:
"Does it exist? Or does it not?"

"What was formerly practiced and cultivated is now loathsome to hear; perhaps it is because of some karmic obstruction that you do not understand. By what means, then, will you maintain the Perfection of Wisdom?
Thus, shrouded by the net of doubt, they find an opportunity for their depravity and instruct other bodhisattvas, saying:
"If this is what you use as the basis for copying and studying, I myself do not yet understand its meaning; how could you possibly understand it?"
He says to himself, "What I practice is right; if what I practice were wrong, my actions would be inverted.
Because of this, that person remains among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, and their transgressions increase day by day.
Thus he is greatly delighted by such perversity.

If a bodhisattva disputes with one who practices the path of proper conduct, or disputes with another bodhisattva, then by speaking such dualistic and perverse words, he distances himself from the Buddha.

If a bodhisattva who has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression should dispute with one who is non-retrogressive, and in accordance with that thought harbor resentment, for every single mental fluctuation, one kalpa is subtracted; yet, despite such evil, they do not abandon the pursuit of omniscience.
"The kalpas are infinite; it must begin from the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "If one has committed evil in the mind, is it possible to repent?"
"Then would one have to wait until the end of that kalpa?
The Buddha said, "My Dharma is vast; one may repent."
If a bodhisattva harbors evil thoughts or resentment, yet delights in instructing others, such a person cannot be made to feel regret.
Should they mistakenly become angry or abusive, they must immediately feel shame and repent their transgression, thinking:
"I shall act as a bridge for the people of the ten directions, enabling them to attain Nirvana."
"How could one harbor ill will and contend with others?
One should endure all evils like a mute sheep.
One should not give rise to anger in the mind for one who follows the path of proper conduct.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells together with these marks, what should the dharma be like?
The Buddha said:
"When looking at one another, you should look as if looking upon the Buddha.
In your minds, you should think:
'We share one teacher, one boat, and one path; what he trains in, I shall also train in.'"
Those who seek the path of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those who delight in desire, I do not share my vows with;
however, those who endure suffering in their quest for Buddhahood, I shall follow and accompany.
"If this is the training in a single dharma.
Chapter Twenty-Two: On Training. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva trains in impermanence, is he training for the sake of all-knowledge?"
"To study non-arising, to study the removal of lust, and to study parinirvāṇa—is this to study all-knowledge?
The Buddha told Śubhavyūha:
"As for what you have asked:"
Regarding the question, "Is it by studying impermanence that one studies all-knowledge?"—
how could the Thus-Come One’s original non-existence be something obtained through causes and conditions?
Since the Thus-Come One is originally without words or letters, how could there ever be a time when he is exhausted?
He replied, “No.
“In this way, one trains in the Perfection of Wisdom for the sake of attaining all-knowledge.”
The ten powers and four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata stage are for the purpose of fully learning all Buddha-dharmas.

"Just as all Buddhas have fully attained the sūtras and dharmas.

While forming this thought for as long as a finger-snap, if one were to practice giving with full perfection for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges River, [the merit would not equal that of the former].
One who practices in this manner dwells on the stage of non-retrogression and is held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Such a person shall never again return to other paths; they will inevitably attain Buddhahood and shall not fall back into the three evil realms.
A bodhisattva never departs from the practice of a Buddha; they should be like the bodhisattva Gandhahastin.
The bodhisattva Gandhahastin was foremost in the land of the Buddha Anabhraka.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: Following Chapter Twenty-Seven. The Bodhisattva Śukla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the bodhisattva follow the teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"No one can destroy the teachings of all the sutras; it is only natural that the bodhisattva follows these instructions.
Space cannot be exhausted, and the five aggregates and four great elements are formless."

The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are fundamentally empty and formless; it is only natural that a bodhisattva follows these teachings. Having resolved their mind to seek Buddhahood with the vow to deliver all sentient beings, their aspiration is vast and universal, beyond compare.
The Buddha has four things that require no protection; each of these is a distinct aspect of his infinitely venerable virtue.
It is natural for a Bodhisattva to follow this teaching, acting as a compassionate protector for sentient beings, and severing all notions of "mine" and "not mine."
Within the void, sounds have no form; yet they accord with the teachings as is natural.

For example, the great ocean cannot be measured by a bushel; like the various wondrous jewels atop Mount Sumeru; like Śakra and Brahmā each having their own instructions; and like the full moon and the bright sun reaching everywhere.
Human beings are fundamentally formless and exist as mere designations; they are fundamentally without birth, being equal to nirvāṇa.
A bodhisattva, following the perfection of wisdom, should regard them as like illusions, transformations, or mirages—possessing names but lacking substantial form.

Just as the four elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are infinite, so too is the physical form of the Buddha fundamentally without color; the realm of the Buddha is fundamentally without boundaries; and the various sūtras and dharmas of the Buddha are fundamentally non-existent, beyond speech, and beyond instruction.
For example, when various birds fly through the air, they leave no tracks.

The five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the concentration of liberation completely transcend all desires; it is only upon reaching the moment of becoming a Buddha that one is able to practice these.

It is natural for the bodhisattva to follow the teachings; the sūtras and dharmas are immeasurable, neither born from anything nor produced by causes. When the time comes for him to become a Buddha, all sūtras and dharmas are fully perfected, and he achieves parinirvāṇa.
Space is non-existent; all sūtras and dharmas are pure and ultimately without cause. The transformations manifested by the Buddha are infinite.
Since there is no bodhisattva who seeks anything, nor anyone who attains Buddhahood, it is only thus that one can deliver countless beings.

The bodhisattva, in accordance with the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā*, should naturally distance himself from flattery, deceit, arrogance, haughtiness, unrighteousness, self-will, wealth, seeking fortune through worldly affairs, and all manner of defilements.
He casts away his body without sparing even his life, seeking nothing for himself, but merely contemplating the Buddha's work to comfort all living beings.
When a bodhisattva’s practice can be thus, he will before long attain Buddhahood; having fully acquired the merit of all-knowledge, he shall be entitled "Buddha."
Why is this? Because he will attain Buddhahood before long.
If there is a bodhisattva who, through this teaching, is destined to receive the title of Buddha in a future age.
Whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, one should likewise follow this Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle Five;
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in the Southern Wu [Kingdom].
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence.
The Buddha addressed Shan Ye:
"If a bodhisattva wishes to swiftly attain Buddhahood, they should seek the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) as the Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence (Samantamaitrī) does.
Shan-ye said: "Where is the Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence now?"
The Buddha said:
"Above, past six hundred and thirty billion buddha-fields, there is a buddha named Gandhottama; his land is called Sarvagandhasugandhā.
He spoke again:
"For what reason does he seek the Perfection of Wisdom?
The Buddha said, "It is because the merit accumulated through his practices in previous lives has fulfilled his original vow; previously, he has already made offerings to countless Buddhas."
At that time, the bodhisattva arose from sleep, and a deva addressed him in a dream, saying:
"If you seek the Great Dharma, seek it immediately upon waking.
He sought it but did not see it; his heart was filled with despondency, and he desired to hear the Great Illuminating Dharma from the Buddha.
At that time, there was no Buddha in the world, nor were there bodhisattvas practicing the pure Dharma in the land; for this reason, he lamented with grief.
It was as if a person had committed an offense against the king, resulting in the forfeiture of all his wealth and property, while his parents and himself were cast into prison.
At that time, a deva from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven looked down and saw the bodhisattva weeping daily;
knowing that he possessed a sincere mind and was striving diligently in his quest for the Way, the deva then taught the bodhisattva how to write characters among his own kinsmen.

"Prior to this time, there was a Buddha in the world named Jingfazihui Laiwang (Jingfa Self-Abased Come-as-King), who had entered parinirvāṇa long ago; [during this interval], they neither beheld the Buddha, nor heard the sutras, nor saw the community of bhikṣus."
Then, again within a dream, he saw a deva from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven tell him:
"There was previously a Buddha named Jingfa (Jingfa-zizui), who came as a king.

Upon hearing the Buddha's name in the dream, he awoke; having awakened, he was filled with great joy. He then left his home, entered the mountains, surrendered his life, and cast away his body, free from all craving or longing. Yet he wept bitterly, reflecting to himself:
"It is due to evil that one does not see the Buddha, does not hear the sutras, and does not attain the dharmas practiced by the bodhisattvas.
At that time, a voice spoke from the air, saying:
"O virtuous one!
Cease, do not grieve so bitterly.
There is a Great Dharma called the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom). If there are those who maintain their resolve and practice it, they will swiftly attain Buddhahood.

If you seek this Dharma, and if you obtain the opportunity to hear and uphold its practice, you shall attain the Buddha’s body of merit, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Once you have attained these, you should likewise teach the Dharma of this sutra to the people of the ten directions.
He asked the voice in the sky:
"By what means was this heard?
To which direction should I go to search for it?"
"What means should be employed?
A voice from the sky replied, "Travel eastward from here; do not rest."

When walking, do not think of left, right, front, back, above, below, or of stopping and moving; do not think of fear or joy, of eating or drinking, of sitting or rising, or of halting while practicing the Way; do not think of lust, anger, or delusion; do not think of guarding one's practice or attaining anything; do not think of the internal and external five aggregates, or of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, or of earth, water, fire, wind, and space; do not think of sentient beings, self, or life-span, nor of existence or non-existence, of the Way or no Way, of the sutras or no sutras, or of being born in the heavens or born in the world.
Bodhisattva!
All thoughts of good and evil are severed and one becomes free from attachment.
If you proceed eastward and practice in this manner without fail, you will soon attain the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

The Buddhas of the past practiced the path of the bodhisattva; seeking in this manner, they attained the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), followed its teachings, and practiced with diligence, thereby surely attaining Buddhahood at an early stage.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva was greatly delighted and said,
"I shall follow the heavenly instruction. He replied:
"Do not lose this instruction.
Having finished speaking, the voice was heard no more.
"Following this instruction, I traveled eastward, remaining free from any discursive thought."
While walking along the path, he thought to himself:
"How much further must I go before I shall attain the Prajñāpāramitā?
He then wept with great sorrow and lamentation.
In the air above, an emanated Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
That which you seek is extremely difficult to attain."
"One who exerts such diligence will attain this before long.

The Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence (Puci) joined his palms and looked up at the transformed Buddha—whose body was golden, who emitted ten billion flames of light, and who possessed the thirty-two marks—and with great joy, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will preach the Dharma."
"I have heard this from the Buddha, and I wish to attain it all.
The Buddha said,
"Receive my teachings and maintain them all with mindfulness."

All dharmas of the various sūtras are fundamentally non-existent and free from fear; they are fundamentally pure and without beginning or end. Abiding in these dharmas of the various sūtras, which are without beginning or end, one dwells in that which is unspeakable and teaches that which is unspeakable.
Like space, it is formless and non-abiding; like nirvana, it is without distinction.
It has no place of origin and is formless and non-abiding; it is like a phantom, like a reflection in water, or like what is seen in a dream—all these are equal and without difference.
Such is the Buddha’s voice; you should follow its teachings to cultivate your resolve and maintain purity.
From here, travel eastward for twenty thousand *li*, and you will reach a land named Gandhavatī, where the Dharma King governs by means of the True Dharma.
That land was prosperous and joyful, with a vast multitude of people.
Its city measured four hundred and eighty li in length and breadth, and was constructed entirely of the seven treasures.
The city had seven concentric walls, between which stood marvelous trees made of the seven treasures; above them were draped canopies of variegated precious gauze that covered the city.
Within it were jeweled lattices from which bells hung; outside each of the four gates of the city stood pavilions for boundless recreation.

Surrounding the city were seven tiers of moats, their waters filled with various kinds of blue lotuses and other famous flowers; their fragrance perfumed the kingdom, and their radiant colors shone afar.
As the practitioner approaches the flowers, his body and robes become like them, all of which grow within the pond.
Upon the dry land between the ponds are *campaka* flowers, *utpala* flowers, and hundreds of such varieties of exquisite blossoms.
In the pond there were various birds—hundreds of species of different kinds such as wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks.
There were boats made of the seven treasures, and the people rode these boats to sport within the pond.
Five-colored banners and streamers were displayed in rows, and canopies of various colors covered the streets and alleys on all sides.

It was like the palace of Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the sound of the suspended banners took the Way and its Virtue as its foundation, never ceasing day or night, so that those who heard it would advance in their practice.
Just like the sounds of music from the *nandanavana* pleasure groves in the heavens, where joy never ceases;
within this city, all are bodhisattvas—some having achieved realization and some having first resolved their minds—whose attire is resplendent and their precious jewels immeasurable.
Among them was a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata, a king among all holy beings, who had six million eight hundred thousand jade maidens as his wives.

All the bodhisattvas constantly paid him respect; in the center of the kingdom, they prepared a high seat, followed by seats of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, arranged in descending order. Upon each of these were spread embroidered silks and fine rugs, and between the seats were scattered various kinds of fragrant flowers. Above them were hung precious canopies, and all around, both inside and out, various famous incenses were burned.

The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata constantly sat upon a high seat to explain the Perfection of Wisdom to the bodhisattvas; among them were those who listened, those who wrote it down, those who studied it, and those who chanted and maintained it.
When you arrive at that place, I shall explain it for you.
For thousands of billions of previous lifetimes, I have always been your teacher; I was the teacher at the very moment you first resolved to attain enlightenment.
When you go to the presence of the Buddha, whatever you hear or see there, be careful not to harbor any doubt or hesitation.
Why is this? If you have not yet awakened to transformative strategies and clear wisdom, you must vigilantly discern and awaken to the nature of evil matters.

A virtuous person is cautious regarding false teachings; do not harbor thoughts that the Teacher is in deep seclusion within the palace and thereby become indolent. You should revere him as you would the Buddha.

Because you employ the Dharma, do not set your mind on wealth or profit; let non-attachment be your treasure, and offer yourself to those you revere, showing compassion and filial piety toward your teachers.
One who practices in this manner shall now attain the Great Dharma.
"Having heard this teaching from the transformation Buddha, the bodhisattva forgets his own body through skillful means and enters the samādhi of beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.
All the Buddhas, from afar, exclaim in praise:
'Excellent, excellent!'"
"Good sir!

When we originally sought the path of the bodhisattva, it was through the power of diligence that we attained the Perfection of Wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and became endowed with all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four ways in which there is nothing to guard, and the eighteen unique qualities; furthermore, we have obtained that which is praised by all Buddhas."
If you seek the traces of the Buddha, you should follow our example.
Those who practice in this manner shall attain the merit of a bodhisattva;
if they do so, they will fully realize it.
The Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence (Puci) arose from his meditative absorption and thought to himself:
"From where do all Buddhas originally come?
Where do they go?"
Having reflected thus, he was again overcome with grief and lamentation, thinking:
"The Buddha has instructed me to go to the place where the Dharma comes.
Thereupon, he departed from there.
He obtained a kingdom through the Middle Way; the kingdom was named Kāmaratī.
While staying overnight in a garden outside the city, he thought to himself:
"The Dharma-jewel of the Buddha is difficult to encounter and hear; I shall exert all my strength to make offerings to the Teacher."
"Now, as for my own person, I am moreover impoverished; I have no precious jewels, incense, or flowers with which to make offerings to the Teacher.
Having had this thought, he entered the city streets and proclaimed himself:
"Who wishes to buy me?"
At that time, Māra was playing outside the city, sporting with ten thousand court ladies.
When Māra heard the sound of the bodhisattva boasting of himself, he thought:

"This bodhisattva has sold his own body, desiring to make offerings to the Dharma; his resolve is set on seeking the Buddha. He shall surely emerge from my realm and deliver a great multitude of people."
‘I shall now destroy this son so that not a single person in the kingdom shall see his form or hear his voice.
Thus it was, and the people within the city could no longer see his form or hear his voice.
"The Bodhisattva, unable to sell himself, rolled upon the ground and wept, crying out:
'I wish to sell myself to serve my teacher, yet there is no one at all who will buy me.'"
"What should be done? Śakra, seeing from afar that the bodhisattva was so diligent, descended to test him, wishing to know whether he sought the Buddha-way with ultimate sincerity.
Was it merely out of flattery?
He then transformed himself into a brahmin and asked,
"Noble sir!..."
"What do you seek that you exert yourself with such toil?
For what reason do you weep so piteously? He replied:
"There is no need to ask.
He asked a second and even a third time:
"Please tell me what you wish to command; I now intend to assist you."
The Bodhisattva replied,
"I am selling my own body to provide for my teacher.
The Brahmin said:
"I wish to perform a great sacrifice and desire to obtain human blood, flesh, marrow, and hearts.
If you can provide these for me, I shall give you even more treasure.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva was greatly delighted in his heart.
He immediately took a knife and pierced both his arms, giving them their blood.
He further cut the flesh from both his thighs and broke his bones to give them the marrow.

Just as he was about to pierce his chest, a daughter of an elder on an upper terrace saw him from afar and felt great pity for him; she came down with five hundred female attendants to the place where the bodhisattva was and asked:
"This noble youth is still so young and upright;
why does he mutilate his own body to such an extent? He replied:
"I shall shed my blood, cut my flesh, and take my marrow to sell them so as to provide for my teacher.
The woman asked,
"If you provide for your teacher in this way, what will you be able to attain?"
"What is the name of that teacher?
Where does he reside?
The bodhisattva replied:
"In the east, there is the one named Dharmodgata; he shall explain the Perfection of Wisdom for me.

Those who hear it should maintain pure conduct, so that they may swiftly attain the thirty-two marks of a Buddha’s body, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four ways in which nothing needs to be guarded, and the eighteen unique qualities; having attained the Wheel of Dharma, they shall turn it to deliver beings throughout the ten directions."
Upon hearing this, the woman was delighted and said,
"As you have said, there is nothing comparable in the heavens above or the earth below.
Why do you subject yourself to such hardship?"
"My son named Bao, together with these women, wishes to follow you to serve the enlightened teacher and to hear the profound sutras.
The bodhisattva said, "Excellent!"
The brahmin said:
"Excellent, excellent!
The noble conduct and diligence of the bodhisattva are difficult to equal."
"I am not a brahmin; I am Śakra, the King of Devas. Therefore, I have come to test you.
What do you seek? I shall grant it all to you. He replied:
"If the Heavenly King has pity on me, may my body be restored.
"May it be as you wish," [he replied]. His sores healed and his body grew strong; his strength exceeded what it was before.
Śakra then departed of his own accord.
The daughter of the elder said to Pucimāṇava, "I wish to see my kinsman; I seek jewels and shall depart.
When the bodhisattva saw her kinsman, the girl related everything to him in detail, and her kinsman said:
"Excellent! I too have had this aspiration;
however, my years are now declining, and my physical body has failed to follow my heart's desire.
If there is something you wish to obtain, please speak of it yourself."
The girl said,
"I wish to obtain rare treasures and exquisite objects.
Her parents said:
"Take as much as you wish," she said.
The woman then took exquisite objects, including woven sandalwood incense and various precious gems; five hundred wagons were so heavily laden that they could not move under their own weight.
Five hundred attendant maidens, accompanied by their respective ladies, addressed the elder’s daughter, saying:
"We wish to serve your noble lady and follow the bodhisattva on his journey.
Her mother granted them permission, and they set out immediately.
Advancing gradually along the road, they saw from afar the Land of Fragrant Purity.

Its cities and ramparts were made of the seven treasures; its banners and streamers shone with brilliant colors; it was adorned with canopies of various jewels, and the sounds of bells and musical instruments resounded. There were pavilions amidst jeweled trees, and various female musicians on chariots and foot; fragrant breezes blew forth in all directions.
For example, when the bodhisattvas and the various goddesses in the heavens see such a sight from afar, their joy is beyond compare.
They think to themselves:
"We ought to alight from our carriage and enter the city on foot.
Together they entered through the western gate and asked a passerby,
"What kind of tower is that?"
"How can his ornaments of the seven treasures be so exquisitely beautiful?
A passerby said, "Does the worthy one not know?
[They belong to the King of Vārāṇasī]."
There was a bodhisattva named Dharmāgata, the most honored among men, whom all worshipped and paid homage to.
By means of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), this bodhisattva constructed this terrace.
Within it was a casket made of the seven treasures, with purple-golden yellow as its base, in which the Prajñāpāramitā was inscribed.

There were hundreds of kinds of famous incenses, and the Dharma-come Bodhisattva daily made offerings—holding various flowers and famous incenses, lighting lamps, hanging banners, flower canopies, and miscellaneous jewels, and playing sublime musical instruments in accordance with the Way, performing every form of reverent offering; the other bodhisattvas did likewise.
"The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven come three times each day and three times each night, bearing celestial flowers to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence (Samantamaitrī) and the women were greatly rejoiced; together they took various incenses and robes woven with golden threads, some scattering them above, some fashioning them into banners, some hanging them on the walls, and some spreading them upon the ground.

When they had finished, they all went together to the assembly hall of the Dharma-āgata Bodhisattva, which was not far away. From a distance, they saw him upon his high seat; he appeared youthful, with a handsome countenance and a radiance that pierced through everything, as he expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* to many hundreds of millions of people.
They met with Dharmodgata and offered him various kinds of incense and many precious robes.
Having performed prostrations and circumambulated him eight hundred times, they took refuge in him and said:
"May we advance in noble conduct and obtain the honored scriptures."
The Bodhisattva Dharmāgata comforted him, saying:
"Congratulations on your arrival; I hope you have not been fatigued?
Whatever you have been commanded to do or whatever you desire to obtain, do not hesitate or feel any doubt."
"I am a teacher who delivers others; I have nothing for which I feel attachment or regret.
The Bodhisattva Universal Compassion said:
"When I was originally seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, I wept with deep sorrow in the mountains."
In the sky there was a manifested Buddha, whose body possessed the thirty-two marks and was the color of purple-polished gold, with ten billion flames of light radiating forth.
The Buddha praised me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The *Prajñāpāramitā* should be sought in this manner.

From here, traveling east for more than twenty thousand *li*, there is a country named Gandhavatī. Within it dwells a bodhisattva named Dharmāgata, the most honored among men, who constantly and repeatedly instructs others.
"If you go there and hear it, you shall attain the *prajñāpāramitā*.
For billions of great kalpas prior, he has constantly been your teacher; he was the teacher when you first resolved upon the path.
Upon hearing the name of my teacher, my heart was filled with such immense joy that I could not contain myself.
Because of this joy, one immediately attains the samādhi of seeing all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, the Buddhas praise me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Our seeking of the Buddha and our pursuit of the Prajñāpāramitā are likewise; we shall personally attain Buddhahood.
Upon waking, however, he was no longer there.
Then I thought to myself:
“From where does the Buddha come?
To where does he go?
I pray that you, O Master, will explain this to me.”
Dharmadatta said: "Worthy one!
Listen well."
Emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness have originally no place from which they come, nor any place to which they go.
The Buddha is likewise: without location, without birth, and without form—like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a person in a dream.
The conceptualization of extinction is without birth, without growth, and without destination.
The fundamental source of the sūtra-realm comes from nowhere, and its departure likewise goes nowhere.
One who wishes to know the Buddha should understand that it is also thus.
“Upon hearing such an immeasurable and profound Dharma as this, the Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence immediately attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi while seated upon his throne.
What are these gates of samādhi?”
The concentration of no fixed location; the concentration of fearlessness amidst liberation from all perversions; the concentration of liberation from the root of craving and desire;
the concentration of deliverance from afflictions and calamities; the concentration of entering into incalculable phrases of the Dharma;
the concentration of the wisdom that enters like the waters of the ocean, which cannot be measured as to their volume; and the concentration of the merit-adornment that adorns Mount Sumeru.

The concentration of observing the formlessness of the five aggregates, the four great elements, and the six sense-fields; the concentration of seeing all Buddhas; the concentration of the bodhisattvas;
the concentration of observing the formless teachings of all the various sutras; the concentration of adorning with precious jewels and observing the entry into those jewels;
the concentration of mindfulness of all Buddhas; the concentration of the bodhisattvas ascending the high seat; and the true stage of non-retrogression.
The wheel of Dharma is the concentration of turning; the adornment of the Buddha’s merits is the concentration; all that is heard without flaw or defilement is the concentration of purity;
all that is heard like the ocean is the concentration; being without attainment and without transgression is the concentration;

the joy of the sound of the sūtras reaching everywhere is the concentration; the manifest banners of the chapters of the sūtra-dharma is the concentration; and the formless body of the Tathāgata is the concentration.
Entering into meditative concentration: the samādhi of formless universal vision found in all sutras; the bodhisattva seal samādhi; the Tathāgata’s eye-witnessing samādhi;
the samādhi of illuminating the spheres of experience; the samādhi of fulfilling the vows of the Buddha-realm; the samādhi of resolving the difficulties of the ten directions;
the samādhi of the adornments of approaching Buddhahood; the samādhi of various flowers of diverse colors; and the samādhi of many precious jewels.
The concentration of the constant turning of the Wheel of Dharma; the concentration of entering the essential through the distant hearing of all sounds;

the concentration of entering the fundamental state of the people of the ten directions; the concentration of reaching everywhere throughout the three realms; the concentration of the various merits of attaining Buddhahood;

the concentration of the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree at the time of no one being able to surpass him in the six perfections; and the concentration of destroying the nets of other non-Buddhist paths.
The Tathāgata beholds the concentration of flying, the concentration adorned with immeasurable merit, the concentration of the merit of wisdom of all precious jewels,
the concentration of the ground of omniscience, the concentration of the complete purification of one’s own mind, the concentration of universal illumination,

the concentration of entering the *nidhi* (treasury) of causes for the people of the ten directions, the concentration emerging from the wisdom of the faculties, and the equality of the three periods of time.
"Samādhi.
In this manner, the Bodhisattva Universal Benevolence attained sixty thousand samādhis.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Coming arose and entered the palace."

"I have come here for the sake of the Dharma."
"The Master is currently within; it is not appropriate for me to sit or lie down.

The women also followed her example and stood up.
At that time, Dharmodgata had just finished instructing the ladies of the inner palace.
Having expounded the path of the sutra, he bathed and washed himself, changed into new clothes, and ascended the Prajñāpāramitā Terrace to sit in contemplation upon various meditative concentrations.
Thus, for seven years, he remained unmoving and unshaken.
The Bodhisattva Samantapriya and all the women likewise practiced walking meditation for seven years, neither sitting nor lying down.
Later, a celestial being spoke to him from mid-air, saying:
"Seven days hence, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata shall arise from his meditative concentration.

"I shall prepare a seat for the Teacher and sweep the ground to make it pure.
They all went to the place where the sutra was being preached and specially prepared a high seat for the Teacher; each of the women took the garments they were wearing and spread them upon the seat.
At that time, Māra thought to himself: "Never before has such a thing occurred.

Because this bodhisattva now offers a high seat out of reverence for his quest for Buddhahood, and because he practices with such diligent vigor and courage, never ceasing or flagging, one who attains the Way shall emerge from my realm and deliver immeasurable sentient beings."
"I shall destroy you!
